title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods

data.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
data.research_question: How do methodological choices in activation patching—corruption methods, evaluation metrics, and sliding-window patching—affect localization and circuit-discovery results, and what are best practices?

To perform STR, we construct PAIRED FACTS of 145 pairs of prompts on factual recall.
For the IOI circuit, we use the pIOI distribution to sample the clean prompts.
We also validate our findings on GPT-J 6B (Wang & Komatsuzaki, 2021) in Appendix G.5.
We take 200 instances of the docstring completion task, perform activation patching by positions and compute the patching effects.
Detections from activation patching on attention heads for the greater-than task in GPT-2 small, averaged across 300 prompts.
We perform activation patching on MLP layers of GPT-2 large in the factual association setting.
Heimersheim & Janiak (2023) studies a circuit for Python docstring completion in a pre-trained 4-layer attention-only Transformer.

protocol.quote: run the model on Xclean and cache activations of a set of given model components, such as MLP or attention heads outputs.

metrics.name: Probability
metrics.definition: Probability of the correct answer; patching effect is patched probability minus corrupted probability.
metrics.quote: Probability: P(r); e.g., P(“Paris”). The patching effect is Ppt (r) − P∗ (r);

metrics.name: Logit difference
metrics.definition: Difference between logits of correct and corrupted answers; patching effect normalized by clean-corrupt logit difference.
metrics.quote: Logit difference: LD(r, r′ ) = Logit(r) − Logit(r′ ); e.g., Logit(“Paris”) − Logit(“Rome”).

metrics.name: KL divergence
metrics.definition: KL divergence from clean output distribution; patching effect is corrupted KL minus patched KL.
metrics.quote: KL divergence: DKL (Pcl ||P ), the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the probability distribution of model outputs in the clean run.

metrics.name: Patching effect
metrics.definition: Restoration of performance after patching; used to rank component importance.
metrics.quote: Patching effect measures how much the patching intervention restores performance, which indicates the importance of the activation.

key_results.claim: In factual-recall MLP localization, GN produces a higher peak than STR across window sizes.
key_results.quote: across window sizes, we find the peak value of GN to be 2×–5× higher than STR

key_results.claim: STR and GN detect inconsistent sets of IOI attention heads.
key_results.quote: Most importantly, we observe that STR and GN produce inconsistent discovery results.

key_results.claim: GN yields a negative detection of head 0.10 in IOI.
key_results.quote: a major anomaly in the GN experiment is the “negative” detection of 0.10.

key_results.claim: Probability overlooks Negative Name Mover head 11.10 under STR.
key_results.quote: both are detected, except when using probability as the metric where 11.10 is overlooked.

key_results.claim: Probability assigns more effect to the last subject token than logit difference under STR.
key_results.quote: Using STR corruption, the ratio is 4.33× in probability > 1.22× in logit difference.

key_results.claim: Sliding-window patching gives higher peak effects than summing single-layer patching.
key_results.quote: Sliding window patching offers 1.40×, 1.75× and 1.59× peak value than summation of single-layer patchings.

key_results.claim: Restoring S-Inhibition values recovers IO logit under STR but not GN.
key_results.quote: we can fully recover model’s logit on IO in STR (logit difference: 1.04) by restoring the values of the S-Inhibition Heads (Figure 3b). The same intervention, however, is fairly unsuccessful under GN (logit difference: 0.49).

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Experiments are limited to decoder-only language models up to 6B parameters.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: our experiments are on decoder-only language models of size up to 6B.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Other architectures and larger models are left for future work.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: We leave it as a future direction to study other architectures and even larger models.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The paper tests only overriding corrupted activations with clean activations.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Our work tests overriding corrupted activations by clean activations.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The reverse direction, patching corrupted to clean, is not compared.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: The other direction—patching corrupted to clean—has also been used for circuit discovery, and it is interesting to compare these two.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Evidence that corruption methods cause OOD behavior is tentative.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: we provide tentative evidence that certain corruption methods lead to OOD model behaviors and suspect that this can make the resulting interpretability claims unreliable.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Further demonstrations of the OOD hypothesis are needed.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Future work should examine this hypothesis closely and furnish further demonstrations.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: The paper studies GPT-2/GPT-J-style decoder-only models, not Gemma 4 E2B; transfer to KV-shared layers 15-34 and per-layer embeddings is untested.
KV-shared layers may make patching assumptions of component independence problematic, because intervening on one layer can affect shared key/value state used by other layers.
CPU-based activation patching on Gemma 4 E2B may have low statistical power; the 2-SD detection rule could be unstable with small prompt samples or noisy metrics.

Per-layer embeddings and logit-lens readouts may interact with corruption choice, so OOD corruption could distort factual-recall and induction-head localization more than the paper’s settings suggest.
The paper’s metrics often assume single-token answers and clean/corrupt answer pairs; Gemma tokenization or multi-token factual answers may break these assumptions.
Sliding-window patching may inflate localization through nonlinear joint effects, and this risk may be larger in KV-shared architectures where layer interactions are structurally coupled.
data.relevance_to_lab: Directly relevant: it gives methodological cautions for activation patching, metric choice, corruption design, and sliding-window patching that should inform CPU-based patching, logit-lens, induction-head, and factual-recall experiments on Gemma 4 E2B, especially because KV-shared layers 15-34 and per-layer embeddings may violate component-independence assumptions.

data.research_question: How do corruption method, evaluation metric, sliding-window patching, and token choice affect activation-patching localization and circuit discovery in language models?

We follow the setting of Stolfo et al. (2023) and perform localization analysis on the task of basic arithmetic in GPT-J (Wang & Komatsuzaki, 2021), a decoder-only model with 6B parameters.

models_and_data.quote: To perform STR in the factual association setting, we construct PAIRED FACTS, a dataset of 145 pairs of prompts.

models_and_data.quote: For the IOI circuit, we use the pIOI distribution to sample the clean prompts.

protocol.step: Run the clean prompt and cache latent activations for the target model components.
protocol.quote: (1) Clean run: run the model on Xclean and cache activations of a set of given model components, such as MLP or attention heads outputs.

protocol.step: Run the corrupted prompt and record its model outputs.
protocol.quote: (2) Corrupted run: run the model on Xcorrupt and record the model outputs.

protocol.step: Rerun the corrupted prompt while restoring one target component's activation from the clean cache.
protocol.quote: (3) Patched run: run the model on Xcorrupt with a specific model component’s activation restored from the cached value of the clean run (Figure 1a).

protocol.step: Create Gaussian-noise corruption by adding N (0, ν) to key-token embeddings, with ν equal to 3 times the textset token-embedding standard deviation.
protocol.quote: GN adds Gaussian noise N (0, ν) to the embeddings of certain key tokens, where ν is 3 times the standard deviation of the token embeddings from the textset.

protocol.step: Create symmetric token-replacement corruption by replacing key tokens with similar tokens of equal sequence length.
protocol.quote: STR replaces the key tokens by similar ones with equal sequence length.

protocol.step: For factual recall, corrupt subject tokens, patch MLP activations at the last subject token, and restore 5 adjacent MLP layers per intervention.
protocol.quote: Following Meng et al. (2022); Hase et al. (2023), at each layer we restore a set of 5 adjacent MLP layers.

protocol.step: For IOI, corrupt S2, patch each attention-head output at all positions, and iterate over all heads.
protocol.quote: Then we patch a single attention head’s output (at all positions) and iterate over all heads in this way.

protocol.step: Classify a head as detected when its patching effect is 2 standard deviations from the mean effect.
protocol.quote: To avoid relying on visual inspection, we say that a head is detected if its patching effect is 2 standard deviation (SD) away from the mean effect.

metrics.name: Probability
metrics.definition: Use the probability P(r) of the correct answer; the patching effect is Ppt(r) − P∗(r).

metrics.name: Logit difference
metrics.definition: Subtract the corrupted-answer logit from the correct-answer logit, compare the patched and corrupted runs, and normalize by the clean-to-corrupted logit-difference gap.
metrics.quote: Logit difference: LD(r, r′ ) = Logit(r) − Logit(r′ ); e.g., Logit(“Paris”) − Logit(“Rome”).

metrics.name: KL divergence
metrics.definition: Measure the change from the corrupted to patched run in KL divergence from the clean output distribution.
metrics.quote: The patching effect is DKL (Pcl ||P∗ ) − DKL (Pcl ||Ppt ).

key_results.claim: In GPT-2 XL factual recall, the peak patching effect under Gaussian-noise corruption was substantially larger than under symmetric token replacement across window sizes.
key_results.quote: This is a robust phenomenon: across window sizes, we find the peak value of GN to be 2×–5× higher than STR; see Appendix G.1 for further plots on GPT-2 XL in this setting.

key_results.claim: For IOI circuit discovery, symmetric replacement and Gaussian noise detected different sets of important heads for any fixed metric.
key_results.quote: In particular, for any fixed metric, STR and GN detect different sets of heads as important, highlighted in Table 1.

key_results.claim: Gaussian-noise corruption disrupted Name Mover attention on IOI sentences, distributing attention between IO and S1.
key_results.quote: On the other hand, with GN corruption, we see that the attention is shared between IO and S1 (0.26 and 0.21).

key_results.claim: Restoring S-Inhibition Head values was relatively unsuccessful under Gaussian-noise corruption.
key_results.quote: The same intervention, however, is fairly unsuccessful under GN (logit difference: 0.49).

key_results.claim: Under STR factual-recall corruption, probability assigned a stronger last-subject-token effect than logit difference.
key_results.quote: • Using STR corruption, the ratio is 4.33× in probability > 1.22× in logit difference.

key_results.claim: Under fully random IOI corruption, the original IO's output probability was negligible.
key_results.quote: First, we observe that the probability of outputting the IO of the original IOI sentence is negligible (5e−4) under this corruption.

key_results.claim: Sliding-window patching produced larger peak effects than aggregating individual single-layer patching effects.
key_results.quote: Sliding window patching offers 1.40×, 1.75× and 1.59× peak value than summation of single-layer patchings.

key_results.claim: Corrupting S1 and IO, rather than S2, allowed most metric-and-corruption combinations to detect the Name Mover heads.
key_results.quote: We find that most combinations of metrics and methods are able to notice all the NMs, when corruption applies to S1 and IO.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The experiments cover decoder-only language models no larger than 6B, leaving other architectures and larger models for future study.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: In terms of limitations, our experiments are on decoder-only language models of size up to 6B.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The study tests restoring clean activations over corrupted ones, but does not compare the reverse corrupted-to-clean direction.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: The other direction—patching corrupted to clean—has also been used for circuit discovery, and it is interesting to compare these two.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The evidence that corruption causes out-of-distribution behavior and unreliable interpretability claims is tentative.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: In addition, we provide tentative evidence that certain corruption methods lead to OOD model behaviors and suspect that this can make the resulting interpretability claims unreliable.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The IOI circuit discovery was incomplete and missed critical components such as Name Mover heads.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: However, the discovery we achieved here appear far from complete, with some critical misses such as NM.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The authors do not characterize all Gaussian-noise localization results as illusory or inflated.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: We do not, though, claim that results from GN are illusory or overly inflated.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Sliding-window patching may capture nonlinear interactions and produce inflated localization plots.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: We speculate that simultaneously patching multiple layers could capture the following non-linear effects and results in inflated localization plots:

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Symmetric token replacement is not always applicable, particularly when token alignment or analogous tokens are unavailable.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: GN may be considered as an alternative when token alignment or lack of analogous tokens makes STR unsuitable.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: No experiments target Gemma 4 E2B or KV-shared layers 15–34, so transfer of layer indices, head roles, and per-layer embedding causal effects is unvalidated.
The 2 SD detection heuristic is not adjusted for the many layer, head, and token comparisons, leaving a false-positive risk.
Results rely on paired facts, synthetic IOI, templated docstrings, greater-than sentences, and arithmetic, so external validity to open-ended factual recall is untested.
STR uses semantically similar prompt pairs; shared lexical or semantic structure can preserve or redistribute the target signal and blur attribution to the subject token.
GPT-2 head labels and roles are not established as transferable to Gemma 4 E2B, particularly for Name Mover, Negative Name Mover, S-Inhibition, and induction-head functions.
No CPU runtime, memory footprint, or implementation cost is reported, so large activation-patching and logit-lens sweeps may be impractical on CPU.
The interventions do not establish causal sufficiency or uniqueness because influential or redundant paths can produce similar patching effects.
Reported averages and thresholded detections can hide prompt-level heterogeneity, rare failure modes, and unstable head rankings.
data.relevance_to_lab: Directly relevant as a protocol and metric-selection reference for Gemma 4 E2B activation patching: the paper supplies the clean, corrupt, and patched workflow; recommends in-distribution STR, normalized logit difference, and single-layer patching before sliding windows; and shows that corruption and token choice can change head localization. Its IOI induction-head and factual-recall analyses can inform Gemma tracing over KV-shared layers 15–34 and per-layer embeddings, including logit-lens validation, but the paper provides no Gemma 4 E2B, KV-sharing, per-layer-embedding, or CPU-feasibility evidence, so transfer and runtime remain unvalidated.
